```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

```{r setup}
library(twocpcont)
```

In a two-group superiority trial with two co-primary continuous endpoints,
the treatment must be shown superior on both endpoints, each tested at the
one-sided level `alpha`. With known variances, the co-primary power is a
bivariate normal probability whose dependence on the sample size cannot be
inverted analytically, so the required sample size is usually found by a
search over candidate sample sizes. `twocpcont_ss()` gives it either by that
search (`method = "bivariate"`) or by a noniterative closed-form formula
(`method = "univariate"`), which needs only the univariate normal
distribution and quantile functions.

## Sample size and power

The example uses the design assumptions of EXPEDITION 1, a Phase III trial of
solanezumab in mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's disease (Doody et al., 2014):
mean differences 1.8 and 3.1, standard deviations 9 and 12, one-sided
significance level 0.025, overall power 0.87 and equal allocation. With a
correlation of 0.5 between the endpoints, the closed form gives

```{r}
ss <- twocpcont_ss(delta1 = 1.8, delta2 = 3.1, sd1 = 9, sd2 = 12,
                   rho = 0.5, r = 1, alpha = 0.025, beta = 0.13,
                   method = "univariate")
ss
```

and the co-primary power at this sample size, evaluated with the bivariate
normal distribution, is

```{r}
pw <- twocpcont_power(n1 = ss$n1, n2 = ss$n2, delta1 = 1.8, delta2 = 3.1,
                      sd1 = 9, sd2 = 12, rho = 0.5, alpha = 0.025)
pw$powerCoprimary
```

The two methods can be compared over several correlations:

```{r}
rhos <- c(0, 0.3, 0.5, 0.8)
N_prop <- sapply(rhos, function(rho) {
  twocpcont_ss(delta1 = 1.8, delta2 = 3.1, sd1 = 9, sd2 = 12, rho = rho,
               alpha = 0.025, beta = 0.13, method = "univariate")$N
})
N_conv <- sapply(rhos, function(rho) {
  twocpcont_ss(delta1 = 1.8, delta2 = 3.1, sd1 = 9, sd2 = 12, rho = rho,
               alpha = 0.025, beta = 0.13, method = "bivariate")$N
})
data.frame(rho = rhos, N_conv = N_conv, N_prop = N_prop)
```

The total sample size decreases from `r N_prop[1]` at a correlation of zero
to `r N_prop[4]` at a correlation of 0.8.

## How much can the correlation reduce the sample size?

The maximum reduction rate `r_max()` bounds the relative reduction of the
sample size, compared with a correlation of zero, that any nonnegative
correlation can bring. It depends only on the significance level, the target
power and the ratio `kappa` of the larger to the smaller standardized effect
size:

```{r}
kappa <- (3.1 / 12) / (1.8 / 9)
r_max(kappa, alpha = 0.025, beta = 0.13)
```

so, whatever the correlation, accounting for it can reduce the sample size
of this design by at most `r round(100 * r_max(kappa, alpha = 0.025, beta = 0.13), 1)`%.
The threshold effect-size ratio `kappa_star()` is the smallest `kappa` for
which this bound is at most a chosen tolerance:

```{r}
kappa_star(epsilon = 0.05, alpha = 0.025, beta = 0.13)
```

Here `kappa` = `r round(kappa, 3)` exceeds the threshold
`r round(kappa_star(epsilon = 0.05, alpha = 0.025, beta = 0.13), 3)` for a
tolerance of 5%, so setting the correlation to zero costs at most 5% of the
sample size.

## Reference

Doody RS, Thomas RG, Farlow M, et al. Phase 3 trials of solanezumab for
mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's disease. *New England Journal of Medicine*
2014; 370(4): 311-321. doi:10.1056/NEJMoa1312889
